title: Two testaments
hookLine: Christians read the Hebrew scriptures as the first part of their own story

lines: THERE WAS NO NEW TESTAMENT YET.
cards: A sabbath day in the synagogue at Nazareth. Jesus, a local man, stands up to read. Someone hands him a scroll of the prophet Isaiah.

He unrolls it, finds a passage about good news for the poor and freedom for captives, reads it aloud, rolls it back up, and sits down. Every eye in the room is on him. Now look at what he was holding.
Not a New Testament. There wasn't one yet; none of it had been written.
The scriptures Jesus read, quoted, prayed and argued from were the Hebrew scriptures, and when the Gospels speak of "the scriptures," this is what they mean.

teach.b: Testament comes from the Latin testamentum, which translates a Greek word, diatheke: covenant, a binding agreement.
So Old Testament and New Testament really mean old covenant and new covenant. And the phrase new covenant comes from the Hebrew scriptures themselves.
The prophet Jeremiah says: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah."

teach.h: THE CUP AT THE LAST SUPPER.
teach.b: Centuries later, at the Last Supper, Jesus picks up a cup and, in the King James words, says: "This cup is the new testament in my blood." That's where the name comes from. Now, old can sound like outdated, used up.
That's not how the church has held it. Early on, a teacher named Marcion wanted to throw out the Hebrew scriptures entirely. The church said no, and kept both.
For Christians, the first testament isn't a warm-up act. It's the first part of their own story: creation, Abraham, the exodus, David, the psalms, the prophets. Jesus lived inside that story.

Out of respect, some Christians and scholars also say the Hebrew Bible, or the First Testament. And Jews read these same scriptures, the Tanakh, as complete in themselves, not as the first half of anything.
Christians read them as leading to Jesus. Both communities hold them sacred, and read them in their own ways. For Christians, the story began long before Bethlehem.

how: Christians read both testaments in worship, often an Old Testament reading, a psalm, a New Testament letter and a Gospel on the same Sunday; some call the first part the Hebrew Bible or First Testament out of respect.

games.q: it's the church's early days. a teacher named Marcion says Christians should throw out the Hebrew scriptures and keep only a few new writings. what does the church do?
o: reject Marcion, and keep both testaments.
games.why: the church rejected Marcion's plan. Christians kept the Hebrew scriptures as the first part of their own story.

practice: If you have a Bible, open it to Psalm 1, only six verses; if not, take one line of it: "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season."
Let the picture come, a tree by a river, roots deep, in no hurry. Jews and Christians both pray the psalms: if you pray, pray the line, and if you don't, stay with the tree.

wordCard.voice: Testament. From the Latin for covenant. The Christian Bible's two halves: the old covenant and the new.

orig.note: Greek: covenant, and also a will. translated into Latin as testamentum.

carryVoice: Your line: the story began long before. Psalm 1 is the doorway into the psalms. Day one hundred twenty-six, done.
